## Part 1: Getting started with Arduino

**Learning outcomes**

- Be familiar with the components of an Arduino microcontroller
- Set up an Arduino sketch in the IDE
- Send and receive digital signals to turn an LED on and off
- Apply different variables to coding elements
- Use `for` loops to control digital signals

Key idea: never put an LED straight across a supply — always add a series
resistor. For a 9 V battery, a 2 V LED and 20 mA:

$$R = \frac{9\,\text{V} - 2\,\text{V}}{0.02\,\text{A}} = 350\,\Omega$$

## Part 2: `analogWrite` and Ohm's law

**Learning outcomes**

- Understand Pulse Width Modulation
- Use the `analogWrite` function to vary voltages
- Construct a voltage divider

The Arduino has 8-bit output resolution ($2^8 = 256$ levels), so 0 → 0 V and
255 → 5 V. To output 1.5 V: $\frac{255}{5\,\text{V}} \times 1.5\,\text{V} \approx 76$.

<iframe src="materials/microcontrollers-part-2.pdf" width="100%" height="600" title="Microcontrollers part 2 slides"></iframe>

## Part 5: Voltage dividers

**Learning outcome:** construct a voltage divider.

$$V_{out} = V_s \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$$

<iframe src="materials/microcontrollers-part-5-voltage-dividers0.pdf" width="100%" height="600" title="Microcontrollers part 5 slides"></iframe>

## Part 6: Potentiometers

**Learning outcome:** use a potentiometer to vary voltages going to the Arduino.

A potentiometer acts as an adjustable voltage divider: turning it moves
$V_{out}$ smoothly between 0 V and the supply voltage.

<iframe src="materials/microcontrollers-part-6-potentiometers.pdf" width="100%" height="600" title="Microcontrollers part 6 slides"></iframe>
